Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel on a mountain ridge above the Urubamba River in southern Peru, believed to have been a royal estate of the emperor Pachacuti and one of the major archaeological sites of the Americas.

The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum on the Yamuna at Agra, India, commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and regarded as one of the best examples of Mughal architecture.
Yann; edited by Jim Carter, CC BY-SA 4.0

Abraham Lincoln (1809–1865) was the 16th president of the United States, who led the Union through the American Civil War from 1861, issued the Emancipation Proclamation and was assassinated in Washington in 1865.

Akbar (1542–1605), born Jalal-ud-Din Muhammad Akbar, was the third Mughal emperor, who reigned from 1556 to 1605, enlarged the empire across much of the Indian subcontinent and governed it through a centralised administration and…
Govardhan / Mir Ali Heravi, Public domain

Alexander III of Macedon, known as Alexander the Great, was king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon from 336 to 323 BCE, who conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire and led his army as far as northwestern India.

Ashoka (c. 304 – 232 BCE) was the third ruler of the Maurya Empire, Emperor of Magadha from c. 268 BCE, who conquered Kalinga and then propagated dhamma through edicts inscribed across the Indian subcontinent, and patronised Buddhism.
Photo Dharma from Sadao, Thailand, CC BY 2.0

Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator (69–30 BCE) was Queen of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt from 51 BCE and its last active ruler, who allied herself with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony and died as Octavian made Egypt a Roman province.

Confucius (c. 551 – c. 479 BCE), born Kong Qiu, was a Chinese philosopher and teacher of the Spring and Autumn period in the state of Lu, whose teachings on morality, family and government became Confucianism.
Anonymous Chinese painter of the Western Han period, Public domain

Cyrus II of Persia (c. 600 – 530 BCE), known as Cyrus the Great, founded the Achaemenid Empire by conquering Media, Lydia and Babylon, and is remembered for a policy of tolerance towards the customs and religions of conquered peoples.

Elizabeth I, the last monarch of the House of Tudor, was Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 to 1603; her reign saw an English Protestant church established, the Spanish Armada defeated and a flowering of English drama.
Genghis Khan (born Temüjin; c. 1162 – 1227) was the founder and first khan of the Mongol Empire, who united the Mongol tribes by 1206 and then conquered large parts of China and Central Asia.

Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) was an Arab scholar, historian and judge, born in Tunis, who served rulers across North Africa and in Granada and wrote the Muqaddimah, an introduction to history regarded as a forerunner of sociology and economics.

Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman and author who conquered Gaul, defeated his rival Pompey in a civil war and ruled the Roman Republic as dictator from 49 BCE until his assassination in 44 BCE.
Ángel M. Felicísimo from Mérida, España, Public domain

Kamehameha I, also known as Kamehameha the Great, was a chief of Hawaiʻi Island who conquered the Hawaiian Islands, completed their unification in 1810 and ruled as the first king of the Kingdom of Hawaii until his death in 1819.

Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci was an Italian painter, draughtsman, engineer and scientist of the High Renaissance, who worked in Florence, Milan, Rome and France and is remembered for the Mona Lisa, The Last Supper and his notebooks.
Attributed to Francesco Melzi, Public domain

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948) was an Indian lawyer and anti-colonial nationalist who used nonviolent resistance to lead the campaign for India's independence from British rule, and whose example later inspired movements for…

Mansa Musa (c. 1280 – c. 1337) was the ninth Mansa of the Mali Empire in West Africa, remembered for his wealth in gold, his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and Timbuktu's growth as a centre of Islamic learning.
attributed to Abraham Cresques, Public domain

Napoleon Bonaparte was a Corsican-born general of the French Revolution who became First Consul in 1799 and was Emperor of the French from 1804 to 1814 and again in 1815, leading campaigns across Europe and enacting lasting legal reforms.

Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013) was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison, negotiated the end of apartheid and served from 1994 to 1999 as the country's first black president.
Kingkongphoto & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel, CC BY-SA 2.0

Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub (c. 1137 – 1193), known as Saladin, was a Sunni ruler of Kurdish origin who founded the Ayyubid dynasty, became the first sultan of Egypt and Syria, and took Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

Simón Bolívar (1783–1830) was a Venezuelan military officer and statesman, known as El Libertador, who led what are now Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru and Venezuela to independence from the Spanish Empire.
Luis Enrique Toro Moreno (1897-1933), Public domain

Wu Zetian (624–705), personal name Wu Zhao, was empress consort and empress dowager of the Tang dynasty and, from 690 to 705, emperor of her own Zhou dynasty, the only undisputed female sovereign in the history of China.
Likely to be Zhang Xuan (张萱), Public domain

Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath, born in Stagira, who founded the Peripatetic school in the Lyceum in Athens and whose works contain the earliest known systematic study of logic.
Charlemagne (748–814) was King of the Franks from 768, King of the Lombards from 774 and emperor from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was crowned in Rome by Pope Leo III.
Charlemagne. Autorité émettrice de monnaie indéterminé. Atelier monétaire. Émetteur, Public domain

Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) was a French peasant's daughter who, claiming divine guidance, helped raise the siege of Orléans and secure the coronation of Charles VII during the Hundred Years' War, and was burned for heresy at Rouen.

Martin Luther (1483–1546) was a German priest, theologian and former Augustinian friar whose Ninety-five Theses of 1517 made him the seminal figure of the Protestant Reformation and whose theological beliefs form the basis of Lutheranism.
Lucas Cranach the Elder, Public domain

Isaac Newton (1643–1727) was an English mathematician, physicist and polymath whose Principia of 1687 set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and who also worked on optics and calculus and served as Master of the Royal Mint.

Catherine II, born the German princess Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst in 1729, overthrew her husband Peter III in 1762 and ruled Russia as empress until 1796, expanding the empire and presiding over the Russian Enlightenment.
Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng or Zhao Zheng in 259 BCE, was the king of Qin who conquered the other warring states by 221 BCE, founded the Qin dynasty and became the first emperor of China.

Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, became Great Khan of the Mongols in 1260, founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and by 1279 completed the conquest of the Song, becoming the first non-Han emperor of all China.

Tokugawa Ieyasu, born Matsudaira Takechiyo in 1543, was a Japanese daimyo who seized power after the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, which ruled Japan from 1603 until 1868.
Hammurabi was the sixth Amorite king of Babylon, reigning from c. 1792 to c. 1750 BCE, who brought almost all of Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule and issued the law code that bears his name.

Ramesses II, known as Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty; he reigned for 66 years from 1279 BCE and is remembered for the Battle of Kadesh, a peace treaty with the Hittites and his monuments.
Suleiman I, known as Suleiman the Magnificent, was the Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, whose long reign of conquest, lawmaking and building is regarded as the peak of the Ottoman Empire's power.

Harun al-Rashid was the fifth Abbasid caliph, who reigned from 786 to 809; his reign is traditionally regarded as the beginning of the Islamic Golden Age and is remembered through the One Thousand and One Nights.

Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Balkhī, known as Rumi, was a thirteenth-century Persian-language Sufi mystic and poet who lived in Konya in Anatolia; he is remembered for the Masnavi and as the figure from whom the Mevlevi Order descends.

Hannibal was a Carthaginian general and statesman who commanded Carthage's forces against the Roman Republic in the Second Punic War, crossed the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE and destroyed a Roman army at Cannae before his defeat at Zama.

Haile Selassie I, born Tafari Makonnen, was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1930 to 1974, remembered for his appeal to the League of Nations against the Italian invasion, his reforms, and his place in Rastafari.
unknown; according to [1] and [2] an official portrait of which b/w copies were distributed by the Ethiopian government, Public domain

Toussaint Louverture was a Haitian general, born into slavery in French Saint-Domingue, who became the most prominent leader of the Haitian Revolution and governor-general for life before dying a prisoner in France in 1803.

George Washington was a Virginia planter who commanded the Continental Army in the American Revolutionary War, presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787 and served as the first president of the United States from 1789 to 1797.

Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui was the ninth Sapa Inca of Cusco in the fifteenth-century Andes, remembered for transforming a small chiefdom into the Inca Empire, rebuilding Cusco and, most archaeologists believe, building Machu Picchu as his…

Liliʻuokalani was the only queen regnant and last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, ruling from 1891 until her overthrow in 1893, and the composer of "Aloha ʻOe" and author of a memoir of her country.
James J. Williams / Adam Cuerden, Public domain

The feudal military government of Japan during the Muromachi period, ruled by the Ashikaga clan from Kyoto, remembered for arts shaped by Zen Buddhism, Noh theatre and its slide into the Sengoku wars.
A Mughal province in North India that its nawabs turned into an independent kingdom, then a British protectorate, until the East India Company annexed it in 1856.
Originally a local artist c. 1780 copying a painting by Zoffany, Public domain
The Tamil empire of the Imperial Cholas, founded by Vijayalaya in 848 in the Kaveri valley, which under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I ruled southern India and raided Srivijaya across the sea.

Company rule in India was the government of the British East India Company over much of the Indian subcontinent from the Battle of Plassey in 1757 until the Crown took over after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
A semi-autonomous Kingdom of Poland created by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 in personal union with the Russian Empire, stripped of its autonomy after the uprisings of 1830 and 1863.
A confederacy of between 150 and 330 Greek city-states under Athenian hegemony, founded in 478 BCE to continue the war against Persia, which became the naval empire known as the Athenian Empire.
The duchy formed in 1525 when the Teutonic Order's Prussian lands were secularised under Albert as a Polish fief; the first Protestant state, it passed to Brandenburg and became a kingdom in 1701.
The Islamic state of Sicily, conquered from the Byzantine Empire by the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya and later ruled by the Kalbid emirs, a prosperous Mediterranean power with Palermo as its capital.

The largest state of the Weimar Republic, a parliamentary democracy governed mostly by Social Democrats, deposed by the Prussian coup of 1932, absorbed by the Nazi regime and abolished by the Allies in 1947.
Free State of Prussia, Public domain
The parliamentary republic that governed France from 1870 to 1940, the longest-lasting French system of government since 1789, which built a vast colonial empire and won the First World War.

A Hellenistic Greek kingdom in Central Asia founded by the Seleucid satrap Diodotus I, remembered for its cities such as Ai-Khanoum, its coinage and its spread of Greek culture towards India and China.
A late medieval sultanate of western India, ruled by the Muzaffarid dynasty from Ahmedabad, remembered for its trade, its navy at Diu and its Indo-Islamic architecture until Akbar annexed it in 1573.
A Second World War Axis puppet state ruled by Ante Pavelić's fascist Ustaše in occupied Yugoslavia from 1941 to 1945, which carried out a genocide against Serbs, Jews and Roma.
The first feudal military government of Japan, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo at Kamakura and later run by the Hōjō regents, remembered for repelling the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281.
A Tatar successor state of the Golden Horde on the Middle Volga, ruled from Kazan over the former lands of Volga Bulgaria until the Tsardom of Russia conquered it in 1552.
The Kingdom of Croatia and Dalmatia in union with Hungary from Coloman's coronation at Biograd in 1102 until Louis II's death at Mohács in 1526, keeping its own Sabor, ban and nobility.
A monarchy under the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen dynasty from 1881 to 1947, which doubled in size after the First World War as Greater Romania and ended with the abdication of King Michael I.
A Balkan monarchy proclaimed in 1882 that doubled its lands in the Balkan Wars, was overrun in World War I and merged in 1918 into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.
A feudal Crusader state founded by the leaders of the Fourth Crusade on Byzantine lands after the sack of Constantinople in 1204, it held the city until the Nicaean recovery of 1261.
The first of the four Southern dynasties of China, founded by the general Liu Yu at Jiankang, remembered for the prosperous Reign of Yuanjia, its wars with Northern Wei and its violent court.

The independent Lithuanian republic declared on 16 February 1918, governed from Kaunas while Poland held Vilnius, authoritarian under Antanas Smetona from 1926, and occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940.
Owned by the National Museum of Lithuania, CC BY-SA 2.5
A province of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, formed from Teutonic Order lands in 1466, self-governing until 1569 and annexed by the Kingdom of Prussia in the partitions of Poland.
A medieval Eastern Orthodox empire proclaimed by Stefan Dušan in 1346, which stretched from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth and broke apart after the death of Stefan Uroš V in 1371.
Unknown 14th century Serbian artist, CC BY-SA 3.0
The second period of the Song dynasty, ruled from Lin'an (now Hangzhou) after the Jin conquest of the north, remembered for its maritime trade, paper money, first permanent navy and Neo-Confucianism.
Thebes was the leading polis of the Boeotian League in central Greece, remembered for Epaminondas's victory over Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE and its destruction by Alexander the Great in 335 BCE.

Tibet was a de facto independent state ruled by the Ganden Phodrang government of the Dalai Lamas from the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912 until its annexation by the People's Republic of China in 1951.

The Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic was a constituent republic of the Soviet Union, ruled by the Communist Party of Ukraine, remembered for the Holodomor, the devastation of the Second World War and its declaration of independence…

The French State, the authoritarian rump state headed by Marshal Philippe Pétain from 1940 to 1944 after the German victory in the Battle of France, which collaborated with Nazi Germany, including in the deportation of Jews.
Imprimerie Draeger à Montrouge en région parisienne, Public domain
Germany's first constitutional republic, from 9 November 1918 to 23 March 1933, remembered for hyperinflation, the Golden Twenties and its collapse into Adolf Hitler's dictatorship.
Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and known as Octavian, was the founder of the Roman Empire and its first emperor from 27 BCE to 14 CE, whose principate opened the era of the Pax Romana.
Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, a Persian philosopher and physician of the Islamic Golden Age who served Iranian courts and wrote The Canon of Medicine and The Book of Healing.

Babur (1483-1530), born Zahīr ud-Dīn Muhammad, was a Timurid prince of Fergana who lost his Central Asian lands, ruled Kabul and in 1526 founded the Mughal Empire in northern India; he is also remembered for his memoir, the Baburnama.

Charles Darwin, an English naturalist and geologist whose voyage on HMS Beagle and decades of research led to On the Origin of Species (1859) and the theory that species descend from common ancestors through natural selection.
Henry Maull (1829–1914) and John Fox (1832–1907) (Maull & Fox) [3]; derivative work by Beao, Public domain

Emperor Meiji (1852-1912), personal name Mutsuhito, reigned over Japan from 1867 to 1912, the years in which the Meiji Restoration ended the Tokugawa shogunate and Japan became an industrialising imperial power that annexed Taiwan and…

Frederick II, King in Prussia and later King of Prussia from 1740 to 1786, who seized Silesia, held it through the Seven Years' War, took part in the First Partition of Poland and patronised the Enlightenment.

Galileo Galilei, an Italian astronomer, physicist and engineer of Pisa, Padua and Florence, whose telescope observations and studies of motion helped found modern science and whose defence of heliocentrism led to his condemnation by the…

Hatshepsut was the sixth pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt, ruling from c. 1479 to c. 1458 BCE first as regent and then as queen regnant, and is remembered for her trade expeditions and building works.

José Rizal (1861-1896) was a Filipino ophthalmologist, writer and reformer of the late Spanish colonial period whose novels Noli Me Tángere and El filibusterismo shaped Filipino nationalism; executed by Spain in 1896, he is popularly…

Justinian I, called Justinian the Great, was Roman emperor at Constantinople from 527 to 565, remembered for reconquering North Africa and Italy, codifying Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis and rebuilding the Hagia Sophia.

Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher, the last of the Five Good Emperors, whose reign saw the Parthian and Marcomannic wars and the Antonine Plague and who wrote the Meditations.

Nzinga Mbande (c. 1583 – 1663), called Ngola Njinga by her people, was queen of the Ambundu kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba in present-day Angola, remembered for decades of war and diplomacy against Portuguese expansion.

Peter I (1672–1725), known as the Great, was tsar of all Russia from 1682 and its first emperor from 1721, remembered for the Great Northern War, the founding of Saint Petersburg and sweeping Westernizing reforms.
Attributed to Jean-Marc Nattier, Public domain

Sejong (1397–1450), known as Sejong the Great, was the fourth king of Joseon, reigning from 1418 to 1450, remembered above all for the creation of Hangul and for a reign of advances in science, medicine and agriculture.
Shaka kaSenzangakhona (c. 1787 – 1828) was king of the Zulu Kingdom from 1816 to 1828, remembered for reorganising the Zulu army and for wars whose part in the Mfecane remains disputed.

Shivaji I (c. 1630-1680), of the Bhonsle family, turned his father's jagir near Pune into the Maratha Kingdom, fought the Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughal Empire with hill forts and guerrilla tactics, and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674.

Sun Yat-sen (1866-1925) was a Chinese physician and revolutionary who led anti-Qing movements from exile, became first provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912 and founded the Kuomintang's political creed, the Three…
上海波尔照相馆, Public domain

Sundiata Keita (c. 1217 – c. 1255) was a Mandinka prince who defeated Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso at Kirina and founded the Mali Empire, remembered above all through the Epic of Sundiata kept by the griots.

Timur, or Tamerlane, a Turco-Mongol conqueror of the Barlas tribe who founded the Timurid Empire in the late 14th century, campaigning from Delhi to Anatolia with great slaughter while patronising scholars and building up Samarkand.

Zheng He, born Ma He, was a Chinese admiral and diplomat of the early Ming dynasty, a eunuch in the service of the Yongle Emperor, who commanded seven treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433.

The Aeneid is a Latin epic poem by Virgil, written between 29 and 19 BCE, telling how the Trojan Aeneas fled Troy and reached Italy to become ancestor of the Romans; it became central to Latin education.

The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex in Granada, begun in 1238 by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, and the only well-preserved palace of the medieval Islamic world.

An embroidered cloth nearly 70 metres long, probably commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux and made in England in the decades after 1066, telling the story of the Norman conquest and the Battle of Hastings.

Beowulf is an anonymous Old English epic of 3,182 alliterative lines, set in 5th- and 6th-century Scandinavia and preserved in a single manuscript of about 975–1025, one of the most important works of Old English literature.

The Book of the Dead is an ancient Egyptian funerary text of magic spells, written mostly on papyrus from the beginning of the New Kingdom to around 50 BCE, meant to guide the dead through the underworld into the afterlife.

Chichen Itza is a large pre-Columbian Maya city in Yucatán, Mexico, a regional capital of the northern Maya lowlands from about 600 to 1100, known for the Temple of Kukulcán, the Great Ball Court and the Sacred Cenote.

The Colosseum is the elliptical amphitheatre in the centre of Rome, begun under Vespasian in 72 and completed under Titus in 80, the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built and a lasting symbol of Imperial Rome.

Ancient Jewish manuscripts of the Second Temple period, dated from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE and found in caves near Qumran between 1946 and 1956, including the oldest surviving copies of biblical books.

Domesday Book is the manuscript record of the Great Survey of much of England and parts of Wales, ordered by William the Conqueror and traditionally dated to 1086, and a primary source for English economic history.
The Forbidden City is the imperial palace complex in the centre of Beijing, built from 1406 to 1420 under the Yongle Emperor and home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors until 1924, now the Palace Museum.

The Great Sphinx of Giza is a limestone statue of a resting sphinx carved from the bedrock of the Giza Plateau, probably under Khufu or Khafre in the Old Kingdom, and the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt.

Great Zimbabwe is the stone-walled city near Masvingo built by ancestral Shona people from the 11th to the 15th century, capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe and the largest of the many 'houses of stone' of southern Africa.
Andrew Moore from Johannesburg, South Africa, CC BY-SA 2.0
A royal charter of rights sealed by King John of England at Runnymede in 1215 to make peace with rebel barons; reissued many times, it later became a symbol of liberty and the rule of law.
Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound., Public domain

The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic attributed to Homer, composed around the 8th or 7th century BCE, which follows Odysseus's ten-year journey home from the Trojan War and stands among the oldest works of literature still read.

The Pantheon is a Roman temple in Rome, first built by Marcus Agrippa under Augustus and rebuilt under Hadrian, probably dedicated about 126; a church since 609, its dome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

Petra is the rock-cut city in southern Jordan that the Nabataeans settled in the 4th century BCE and made their capital, a trading hub on the incense routes known for its carved sandstone façades and water systems.

The Ramayana is a Sanskrit epic of ancient India, traditionally attributed to Valmiki, which tells the life and journey of Rama, prince of Ayodhya, and has shaped Hindu life and the arts of South and Southeast Asia.
Scribes and painters employed by the Kingdom of Mewar., Public domain
A granodiorite stele inscribed in 196 BCE with a decree of Egyptian priests for King Ptolemy V in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, whose three versions became the key to deciphering Egyptian writing.

A prehistoric megalithic monument on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, built in phases from about 3100 BCE to about 1600 BCE by a people without writing, and aligned on the solstice sunrise and sunset.

The Tao Te Ching, or Laozi, is an ancient Chinese classic traditionally attributed to the sage Laozi and compiled during the Warring States period, the foundational text of Taoism and one of the most translated works in the world.

The Apache are Southern Athabaskan-speaking peoples of the American Southwest, the Southern Plains and Northern Mexico, who call themselves Indé, resisted Spanish, Mexican and American invasion for centuries and live today in…

The Chamorro, or CHamoru, are the Indigenous people of the Mariana Islands in Micronesia, seafarers who arrived about 1,500 BCE, built on latte stones, and today live on Guam, the Northern Marianas and across the United States.
Photo Dharma from Penang, Malaysia, CC BY 2.0

The Cimmerians were an Eastern Iranic equestrian nomadic people of the Caspian and Ciscaucasian steppes who crossed the Caucasus in the 8th century BCE and shook Urartu, Phrygia, Lydia and the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

The Corded Ware culture was a broad archaeological horizon of northern, central and eastern Europe between about 2900 and 2300 BCE, named for its cord-impressed pottery and thought a likely vector of Indo-European languages.

The Cycladic culture was a Bronze Age culture of the Cyclades in the Aegean Sea, c. 3100–1000 BCE, best known for its schematic white marble figurines and for the seafaring that linked its small island communities.
The Garamantes were an ancient people of the Fezzan in southern Libya who, from at least 1000 BCE to the late 7th century CE, built a desert kingdom on qanat irrigation and trans-Saharan trade.

The Guaraní are culturally related Indigenous peoples of South America, distinguished by the Guarani language, whose traditional range lies in Paraguay, Misiones, southern Brazil, Uruguay and Bolivia, and who number around 280,000 today.

The Haudenosaunee, "those who build the longhouse", also called the Iroquois or Six Nations, are a confederacy of Iroquoian peoples of northeast North America, united under the Great Law of Peace and still governed by their Grand Council.

The Jurchens were Tungusic-speaking peoples of Manchuria, first recorded in 748, who founded the Jin dynasty (1115–1234) and, under Nurhaci, the Later Jin, before Hong Taiji renamed them Manchus in 1635.

The Linear Pottery culture (LBK) was a Neolithic archaeological horizon of central Europe, c. 5500–4500 BCE, whose farmers spread agriculture along the Danube, Elbe and Rhine and built the largest free-standing buildings of their time,…

The Nubians are a people indigenous to Nubia, the Nile valley from southern Egypt to northern Sudan, who speak Nubian languages, built the kingdoms of Kush and Christian Nubia, and live today in Egypt and Sudan.
The Picts were a group of peoples in what is now Scotland north of the Firth of Forth in the Early Middle Ages, remembered for their carved symbol stones, their silverwork and the kingdom of Fortriu.

Tartessos was a civilisation of the southern Iberian Peninsula, from the late Bronze Age to the 5th century BCE, rich in metals, trading with Phoenicians and Greeks, and writing in the Southwest script.

The Tlingit, or Lingít, are an Indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest Coast, Alaska Natives and First Nations in Canada, known for their matrilineal clans, crest art and a hunting, fishing and gathering life built on rich fisheries.

The Vinča culture was a Neolithic culture of the central Balkans, 5400–4500 BCE, known for some of the largest settlements of prehistoric Europe, dark-burnished pottery, figurines, the Vinča symbols and the earliest known copper smelting.
The Zapotec civilisation flourished in the Valley of Oaxaca in Mesoamerica from about 700 BCE to 1521 CE, with Monte Albán, one of the first major cities of Mesoamerica, as the centre of its state.

The Soviet republic of Armenia, with its capital at Yerevan, created by the Sovietisation of the First Republic in 1920, which grew from an agricultural hinterland into an industrial centre and became independent in 1991.
The communist state proclaimed by Hồ Chí Minh in Hanoi in 1945, which defeated France at Điện Biên Phủ, ruled the North after the partition of 1954 and conquered the South in 1975.
An Iron Age kingdom in the south of present-day Jordan, east of the Arabah, remembered for its copper mines, its god Qaus and its long rivalry with Israel and Judah in the Hebrew Bible.

The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the federation of Serbia and Montenegro formed in 1992 after the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, remembered for sanctions, hyperinflation and the Kosovo War.
U.S. Air Force/Staff Sgt. Brian Schlumbohm, Public domain

The Spanish State ruled by Francisco Franco, first in the Nationalist-held territories during the Spanish Civil War and then over all Spain until his death in 1975, a single-party dictatorship of National Catholicism and repression.

The republic founded in 1792 during the French Revolution, which abolished the monarchy, executed Louis XVI, passed through the Reign of Terror, the Directory and the Consulate, and ended with Napoleon's empire in 1804.

The German colony of the African Great Lakes region, taking in present-day mainland Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, remembered for the violence of its conquest, the Maji Maji Rebellion and Lettow-Vorbeck's wartime campaign.
Photoatelier Hermann Noack, Berlin; cropped, retouched and resolution reduced by Jossi2, Public domain

The Kingdom of Cambodia of 1953–1970, the Sangkum period, was Norodom Sihanouk's first administration, from independence from France to the coup of 1970, remembered for his one-party rule and his neutrality in the Vietnam War.
(unknown, Abaca Press claims ownership but claim is doubtful), Public domain
A kingdom of the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula, formed in the partition of 910 and later joined to León and Castile, centred on the pilgrim city of Santiago de Compostela and dissolved in 1833.
The kingdom without a king that the Regent Miklós Horthy ruled from 1920 to 1946, shaped by the losses of the Treaty of Trianon, which joined the Axis and took part in the Holocaust.

Korea as a colony of the Empire of Japan under the name Chōsen, ruled by a Governor-General in Keijō from the annexation of 1910 until Japan's surrender in 1945, and remembered for forced assimilation, extraction and mass mobilisation.
This photo was taken in 1907., Public domain

The Marcomanni were a Suebian Germanic people beside the Roman Danube frontier, recorded from 58 BCE to about 400 CE, remembered for the Bohemian kingdom of Maroboduus and the Marcomannic Wars against Marcus Aurelius.

The British protectorate north of the Zambezi, ruled by the British South Africa Company until 1924 and then by the Crown, whose Copperbelt mines made it rich and which became independent as Zambia in 1964.

The Pechenegs were a semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who controlled much of the steppes of southeast Europe and the Crimean Peninsula in the 9th and 10th centuries, raiding Kievan Rus' and serving Byzantium.
Portugal's colony on the Atlantic coast of west-central Africa, founded at Luanda in 1575, for two centuries a great slave-trading enterprise tied to Brazil, and independent as Angola in 1975.

The anti-communist state of southern Vietnam, proclaimed by Ngô Đình Diệm in 1955 after the partition at the 17th parallel, which fought the Vietnam War with American support until the fall of Saigon in 1975.
U.S. Air Force (Operation Holly 1970 (Folder 13 of 15), sheet 182), Public domain

The Polish state reborn at the end of the First World War after more than a century of partitions, which won the Polish–Soviet War, fell under Piłsudski's Sanacja regime and was destroyed by the German and Soviet invasions of 1939.
The democratic republic that governed Spain from the deposition of King Alfonso XIII in 1931 until its defeat by the Nationalist rebels of General Francisco Franco in the Spanish Civil War in 1939.

The southern branch of the Xiongnu, formed when eight tribes broke from the chanyu Punu in 48 and settled inside Han China's northern frontier as tributary auxiliaries until Cao Cao ended the chanyu's court.
Spain's province of La Florida in south-eastern North America, centred on St.

Pericles (c. 495–429 BCE) was an Athenian statesman and general who led Athens from about 461 BCE until his death, turned the Delian League into an Athenian empire and began the building programme of the Acropolis.

Constantine I, known as Constantine the Great (272–337), was Roman emperor from 306 and sole ruler from 324, the first emperor to convert to Christianity, who legalised the faith and founded Constantinople as the empire's capital.

Theodora (c. 495–548), a bear keeper's daughter and former actress, was the wife of Justinian I and Eastern Roman empress from 527, one of his chief political advisers and a protector of the Miaphysite Christians.

Mehmed II, known as Mehmed the Conqueror (1432–1481), was Ottoman sultan in 1444–1446 and from 1451 to 1481, who took Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and rebuilt it as his imperial capital.

Isabella I, known as Isabella the Catholic (1451–1504), was Queen of Castile and León from 1474 who, with her husband Ferdinand II of Aragon, conquered Granada, expelled Spain's Jews and sponsored Columbus's voyage of 1492.

Christopher Columbus (1451–1506) was a navigator from the Republic of Genoa whose four voyages for the Catholic Monarchs of Spain, from 1492, began lasting European contact with the Americas, and whose governorship of Hispaniola was…

Moctezuma Xocoyotzin (c. 1466–1520), known as Moctezuma II, was the ninth emperor of the Aztec Empire, which reached its greatest size under him, and was its ruler when Hernán Cortés and the Spaniards entered Tenochtitlan in 1519.

Atahualpa (c. 1502–1533), Atawallpa in Quechua, was the last effective Inca emperor, who won the throne from his half-brother Huáscar in a civil war and was captured at Cajamarca and executed by Francisco Pizarro's Spaniards.

Otto von Bismarck (1815–1898), a Prussian Junker who became minister president of Prussia in 1862, unified Germany through three wars and governed the German Empire as its first chancellor from 1871 until Wilhelm II dismissed him in 1890.

Victoria (1819–1901) was Queen of the United Kingdom from 1837 and Empress of India from 1876, whose reign of more than 63 years gave its name to the Victorian era of industrial change and imperial expansion.

Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882) was an Italian general, revolutionary and republican from Nice who fought in South America and Europe, led the Expedition of the Thousand in 1860 and is remembered as a maker of Italian unification.

Harriet Tubman (c. 1822–1913) was an American abolitionist who escaped slavery in Maryland, led some 70 enslaved people to freedom on the Underground Railroad, served the Union Army as a scout and spy and campaigned for women's suffrage.

Frederick Douglass (c. 1818–1895) was an American abolitionist, orator, writer and statesman who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838, wrote three autobiographies and became the leading figure of the African-American civil rights…

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (c. 1881–1938) was an Ottoman officer who led the Turkish War of Independence, founded the Republic of Turkey and, as its first president from 1923 to 1938, imposed sweeping secular reforms under one-party rule.

Ho Chi Minh (Hồ Chí Minh, 1890–1969) was a Vietnamese communist revolutionary who founded the Indochinese Communist Party, led the Việt Minh against Japan and France and ruled North Vietnam as its president from 1946 until his death.

Mao Zedong was a Chinese revolutionary and political theorist who led the Chinese Communist Party to power, founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and was its paramount leader until his death in 1976.

Sir Winston Churchill was a British statesman, soldier and writer, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 and again from 1951 to 1955, remembered above all as Britain's leader in the Second World War.

Jawaharlal Nehru was an Indian lawyer, nationalist and statesman, a principal leader of the independence movement and India's first prime minister from 1947 until his death in 1964, remembered for parliamentary democracy, secularism and…

Kwame Nkrumah was a Ghanaian politician and Pan-Africanist who led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana in 1957, the first in sub-Saharan Africa, and ruled it, latterly as a one-party state, until a coup in 1966.

Ibn Battuta was a Maghrebi Muslim traveller and scholar from Tangier who between 1325 and 1354 visited much of Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula, and is remembered for the account of his journeys known as the Rihla.
Jesus was a Jewish preacher and religious leader of Galilee and Judaea in the first century, whom Christians hold to be the Messiah and the Son of God and from whose followers Christianity grew.

Muhammad was an Arab religious, military and political leader of Mecca and Medina in the early 7th century, whom Muslims hold to be the final prophet of God and whose reported revelations form the Quran.
Bluemangoa2z at Malayalam Wikipedia, Public domain

Siddhartha Gautama, called the Buddha, was a wandering religious teacher of the eastern Indo-Gangetic Plains in the 6th or 5th century BCE, remembered as the founder of Buddhism and its teacher of a Middle Way.
พระมหาเทวประภาส วชิรญาณเมธี (ผู้ถ่าย-ปล่อยสัญญาอนุญาตภาพให้นำไปใช้ได้เพื่อการศึกษาโดยอยู่ภา่ยใต้ cc-by-sa-3.0) …, CC BY-SA 3.0
Moses is the Hebrew prophet who, according to the Book of Exodus, led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt and received the Mosaic Law, which forms part of the Torah.

Zoroaster, or Zarathustra Spitama, was an Iranian religious reformer and poet-prophet, traditionally the author of the Gathas, who is regarded as the spiritual founder of Zoroastrianism; his dates and homeland are uncertain.
dates disputed: c. 1000 BCE, or 7th–6th century BCE

Guru Nanak was an Indian spiritual teacher, mystic and poet of Punjab, born in 1469, regarded as the founder of Sikhism and the first of its ten gurus, who taught devotion to one God and the equality of all people.
Amritpal Singh Mann. Painted by Jaimal Singh Naqqash (1860–1916), Mehtab Singh Naqqash (1871–1940), and Hukum Singh., CC BY-SA 4.0

Laozi, the 'Old Master', is the figure traditionally held to be the author of the Tao Te Ching and the founder of Taoism; scholars doubt that he lived as the tradition tells, and the book is generally seen as the work of several hands.

Mahavira, born Vardhamana, was an Indian religious reformer of the 6th or 5th century BCE, whom Jains hold to be the 24th and last Tirthankara of the present time cycle, and who is remembered for teaching ahimsa.

Paul, born Saul of Tarsus, was a first-century Jewish Christian apostle who spread the teachings of Jesus to non-Jewish communities in Asia Minor and Europe and whose letters form a large part of the New Testament.
Ali ibn Abi Talib was the cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, the fourth Rashidun caliph from 656 to 661 and, for Shia Muslims, the first Imam and rightful successor to the Prophet.
U.S. Navy photo by Photographer's Mate 1st Class Arlo K. Abrahamson., Public domain

Abraham is the patriarch of the Book of Genesis, revered in Judaism, Christianity and Islam as father of the Jewish and Arab peoples; most scholars treat the patriarchal age as a late literary construct.
placed by tradition in the early 2nd millennium BCE

Mary was a first-century Jewish woman of Nazareth, the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus, venerated in Christianity under many titles and honoured in Islam, where a chapter of the Quran bears her name.

The Hebrew Bible is the canonical collection of Hebrew scriptures, the Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim, composed and edited by the Israelites over several hundred years; its authoritative Jewish form was fixed in the Masoretic Text of the…

The New Testament is the second division of the Christian Bible: 27 texts in Koine Greek by various authors, including four gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation, mostly written in the mid to late first century and settled as a canon by…

The Quran, in Arabic the 'recitation', is the central religious text of Islam, which Muslims believe was revealed by God to Muhammad over some 23 years from 610 CE, and which is also studied as a text of Arabic literature.
The Rigveda is a collection of 1,028 Vedic Sanskrit hymns, composed most likely between c. 1500 and 1000 BCE in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent.

The Bhagavad Gita is a Hindu scripture of 700 verses, part of the Mahabharata and likely composed in the second or first century BCE, in which Krishna advises the warrior Arjuna on duty, knowledge and devotion before the Kurukshetra War.

The Pāḷi Canon is the standard collection of scriptures of Theravada Buddhism, preserved in the Pāli language and divided into three baskets, the Tipiṭaka; it is the most complete extant early Buddhist canon.

The Avesta is the corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, composed orally in the Avestan language over several centuries, written down in the Sasanian era, and now surviving only in part in ritual and devotional manuscripts.
The Guru Granth Sahib is the central scripture of Sikhism, which Sikhs regard as their final and eternal Guru.

The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism after the Hebrew Bible: the Mishnah and the Gemara's commentary on it, compiled in Galilee and Babylonia between the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE and the early seventh century.

The Upanishads are Sanskrit texts of the late Vedic and post-Vedic periods, composed in northern India and the most recent addition to the Vedas; the oldest are placed in the 7th to 6th centuries BCE.

The Lotus Sūtra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture by unknown Indian authors, composed in phases from about the 1st century CE, and the main text of the Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren schools of East Asia.
Text inscribed by Sugawara Mitsushige, Public domain

The I Ching or Yijing, the Book of Changes, is an ancient Chinese divination text built on 64 hexagrams, later joined to the Ten Wings commentaries and made one of the Five Classics in the 2nd century BCE.
Song era print artist, Public domain
Alexandria is a port city on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, at the western edge of the Nile Delta.
Babylon was an ancient city on the lower Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, near modern Hillah in Iraq.
Baghdad is the capital of Iraq, on the Tigris.
Beijing is the capital of China, in the north of the country.
Cairo is the capital of Egypt, on the Nile where the valley opens into the Delta.
Ahmed Al.Badawy from Cairo, Egypt, CC BY-SA 2.0

Chang’an was a capital of Chinese dynasties in Shaanxi from the Western Han to the Tang, in two walled cities on nearby sites, and was at times the largest city in the world; Xi’an stands there today.
Unknown Tang-era tomb artist, Public domain

Constantinople is a city on the Bosphorus in south-eastern Europe, settled by Greek colonists as Byzantium around 657 BCE, refounded by Constantine as Constantinople, capital of the Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires, and now Istanbul.
Cusco is a city in the Andes of south-eastern Peru, at about 3,400 metres, founded in the 12th century according to tradition and for centuries the capital of the Inca Empire.

Delhi is a city on the Yamuna river in northern India, with a recorded history from the Tomara rulers of the 11th century, the capital of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, and now of the Republic of India.

Isfahan is a city in central Iran on the Zayandeh River, a regional centre under the Medes and a capital under the Parthians, Seljuks and Safavids, best known for the square and boulevard of Abbas the Great.
Jerusalem is a city on a plateau in the Judaean Mountains, first settled near the Gihon Spring around 3000 BCE, and holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam, whose status is disputed today.
Kyoto is a city in the Yamashiro Basin on Honshu, Japan, founded in 794 as Heian-kyō, the seat of the imperial court for more than a thousand years, and now the capital of Kyoto Prefecture.
Nina R from Africa, CC BY 2.0

London is the capital of England and the United Kingdom, on the River Thames in south-east England, founded by the Romans as Londinium about 47 CE and since a major port, seat of government and commercial centre.

Mecca is a city in the Hejaz of western Saudi Arabia, 70 km inland from Jeddah, the birthplace of Muhammad and the holiest city of Islam, whose Kaaba is the direction of prayer for Muslims and the goal of the Hajj.
5th century CE – present; by tradition far older
Paris is the capital of France, on the Seine.
Yann Caradec from Paris, France, CC BY-SA 2.0
Rome is the capital and largest city of Italy, on the Tiber in Lazio.
Samarkand is a city in the Zarafshan valley of south-eastern Uzbekistan, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of Central Asia, a Sogdian city, a Silk Road centre and the capital of Timur.
Gustavo Jeronimo from Aranjuez, Spain; derivative work by MrPanyGoff, CC BY 2.0

Tenochtitlan was the Mexica capital on an island in Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, founded in 1325 by the date now accepted, capital of the Aztec Empire, and captured by the Tlaxcaltec and the Spanish in 1521.

Timbuktu is a city in Mali, 20 kilometres north of the Niger River, which began as a seasonal Tuareg camp about 1100 CE and became a trading and Islamic scholarly centre under the Mali and Songhai empires.
Flickr Emilio Labrador Santiago de Chile 3059349393 (Flickr), CC BY 2.0

Venice is a city on a group of islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic in north-eastern Italy, traditionally founded in 421, and for almost a thousand years the capital of a maritime republic.

On 1 March 1896 an Ethiopian army under Emperor Menelik II defeated an Italian colonial force under General Oreste Baratieri near Adwa, ending the First Italo-Ethiopian War and leading Italy to recognise Ethiopian sovereignty in the…

On 25 October 1415 Henry V's English army, marching to Calais and heavily outnumbered, defeated a French army near Azincourt in northern France, a victory that gave England the advantage in the Hundred Years' War for some years.

On 3 September 1260 the Bahri Mamluks of Egypt under Sultan Qutuz defeated a Mongol force of the Ilkhanate under Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut in the Jezreel Valley, and the Mamluks then took Damascus and Aleppo.
On 13 March 624 CE (17 Ramadan, 2 AH) Muhammad's followers from Medina defeated a larger Qurayshi army from Mecca near Badr, killing several Meccan leaders and strengthening Muhammad's position.
Hannibal's Carthaginian army surrounded and destroyed most of a larger Roman and allied army under the consuls Paullus and Varro at Cannae in Apulia in 216 BCE, during the Second Punic War.
Alexander the Great and the army of Macedon defeated the Persian army of Darius III at Gaugamela, north of Arbela in what is now Iraq, in 331 BCE; the Achaemenid Empire fell soon after.
Union forces under George Meade defeated Robert E. Lee's Confederate army at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, from 1 to 3 July 1863, ending Lee's invasion of the North and forcing his retreat to Virginia.
Thure de Thulstrup / Adam Cuerden, Public domain
On 14 October 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English army of King Harold Godwinson about 7 miles northwest of Hastings; Harold was killed, and William was crowned king on Christmas Day.

On 4 July 1187 the army of the Crusader states, under King Guy of Jerusalem, was surrounded and broken near Tiberias by Saladin's forces, which then took Jerusalem and most Crusader-held towns and prompted the Third Crusade.

Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire fought on the Orontes near Kadesh after a Hittite attack nearly broke the Egyptian army; both sides claimed victory and the Hittites kept Kadesh.

On 7 October 1571 the Holy League fleet under John of Austria defeated the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras; the Ottomans rebuilt quickly, and Venice made peace with them in 1573 and gave up Cyprus.
The Athenians, helped by Plataea, defeated a Persian force under Datis and Artaphernes on the plain of Marathon in Attica in 490 BCE, ending the first Persian invasion of Greece.

On 23 June 1757 Robert Clive's East India Company force beat the army of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey in Bengal, helped by the inaction of commanders who had conspired with the Company; Mir Jafar was made Nawab.
On 21 October 1600 the forces of Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated a coalition led by Ishida Mitsunari in what is now Gifu Prefecture after several commanders defected; Ieyasu became shōgun in 1603.
User LordAmeth on en.wikipediaCollection of The Town of Sekigahara Archive of History and Cultural Anthropology, Public domain

The Soviet Union defeated Germany and its Axis allies at Stalingrad on the Volga between 1942 and 1943; the German 6th Army was encircled and surrendered, and the strategic initiative on the Eastern Front passed to the Red Army.

On 18 June 1815 a French army under Napoleon was defeated near Waterloo, in present-day Belgium, by a British-led army under Wellington and a Prussian army under Blücher; Napoleon abdicated again four days later.

The Ottoman army under Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople for 53 days and took the Byzantine capital on 29 May 1453, after which the city was sacked and became the Ottoman capital; the fate of Emperor Constantine XI is unknown.
On 14 January 1761 the Durrani Empire and its Indian allies defeated the Maratha army at Panipat, 97 kilometres north of Delhi; tens of thousands of Marathas died in the fighting and after it.

Octavian's fleet under Marcus Agrippa defeated the combined fleets of Mark Antony and Cleopatra off Actium in the Ionian Sea in 31 BCE, after which both took their own lives and Octavian became sole master of Rome.
In November 636 the army of the Rashidun Caliphate defeated the Sasanian army of Rustam Farrokhzad at al-Qadisiyyah in Iraq, after which Ctesiphon fell and the Sasanians lost Mesopotamia.

The Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur defeated King Alfonso VIII of Castile at Alarcos, near the Guadiana, on 18 July 1195, and Castile's field army was destroyed, leaving the road to Toledo open.

Julius Caesar's Roman army besieged the Gallic leader Vercingetorix and his allies in the fortified settlement of Alesia in September 52 BCE, beat off a Gallic relief force, and ended organised Gallic resistance.

Napoleon's Grande Armée defeated a combined Russian and Austrian army near Austerlitz in Moravia on 2 December 1805, in the War of the Third Coalition, and Austria then left the war by the Treaty of Pressburg.

On the Pampa de Ayacucho in the Peruvian highlands, Antonio José de Sucre's United Liberation Army defeated the royalist army of Viceroy José de la Serna, who was wounded and captured, and the royalists capitulated, ending Spanish rule…
Martín Tovar y Tovar, Public domain

A combined Venezuelan and New Granadan army with a British Legion under Simón Bolívar defeated Colonel José María Barreiro's Spanish III Division at Boyacá in 1819, opening the road to Santa Fe and the founding of Gran Colombia.
Martin Tovar y Tovar, Public domain

Austro-Hungarian forces reinforced by German units broke through the Italian line near Kobarid on the Isonzo front in October 1917, routed the Italian Second Army and drove the Italian army back to the Piave river.

A Parthian cavalry army under Surena defeated the Roman army of Marcus Licinius Crassus near Carrhae in 53 BCE; Crassus was killed, most of his men were killed or captured, and Parthia later invaded Syria and Armenia.

An English army under Edward III, standing on a hillside near Crécy-en-Ponthieu in northern France, beat off repeated attacks by a much larger French army under Philip VI in 1346, during the Hundred Years' War, and went on to take Calais.

Viet Minh forces under Võ Nguyên Giáp besieged and overran a French Union garrison in the valley of Điện Biên Phủ in northwest Tonkin in 1954, in the First Indochina War, and French withdrawal from Indochina followed.

The Polish and Lithuanian army under Władysław II Jagiełło and Vytautas defeated the Teutonic Order under Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen near Grunwald in 1410, killing him and much of the Order's leadership.

In 200 CE, late in the Eastern Han dynasty, the warlord Cao Cao held the fortified camp at Guandu against the larger army of Yuan Shao, burned Yuan's grain at Wuchao and routed him, becoming the dominant power in northern China.

A Zulu army of some 20,000 overran part of the British main column at Isandlwana in Zululand on 22 January 1879, early in the Anglo-Zulu War, killing over 1,300 troops and bringing a larger second British invasion.

Alexander the Great's Hellenic League army defeated the Achaemenid army of Darius III near the Pinarus river by Issus in southern Anatolia in 333 BCE, and Darius fled, leaving his family and treasury to be captured.

American Marines, Navy and Army forces landed on Iwo Jima in the Volcano Islands in February 1945 and took it from the Japanese garrison under Kuribayashi in five weeks, at a cost in casualties higher than the Japanese suffered.

On 14 October 1806 Napoleon's army defeated Prince Hohenlohe's Prussians at Jena while Marshal Davout's single corps beat the main Prussian army at Auerstedt, in the War of the Fourth Coalition; Prussia's resistance collapsed in the…

The British Grand Fleet under Jellicoe and the German High Seas Fleet under Scheer fought off the Danish coast of Jutland in 1916; Britain lost more ships and men, but the German fleet returned to port and stayed there.

On 10 October 680 at Karbala in southern Iraq, the army of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I killed Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad, and most of his small party, with consequences for the Second Fitna and for Shia identity.
A British and Indian garrison held Kohima ridge against the Japanese 31st Division in April 1944, was relieved, and with reinforcements drove the Japanese off, reopening the road to Imphal in June.
Official photographer of No.9 Army Film and Photographic Unit., Public domain

On 3 July 1866 the Prussian armies defeated the Austrian army of Ludwig von Benedek near Königgrätz in Bohemia, the decisive battle of the Austro-Prussian War, which cleared the way for a German state without Austria.

An Ottoman army under Sultan Murad I fought an army led by the Serbian Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović on the Kosovo field in 1389; both leaders died, both armies were badly weakened, and the Serbian principalities later became Ottoman vassals.

In the summer of 1943 German forces attacked the Kursk salient on the Eastern Front, were stopped by deep Soviet defences, and were then driven back by Soviet counter-offensives that left the Red Army holding the strategic initiative.

Hannibal's Carthaginian army ambushed a Roman army under the consul Gaius Flaminius on the north shore of Lake Trasimene in 217 BCE, during the Second Punic War, and killed or captured nearly all of it.
The armies of the Sixth Coalition, from Austria, Prussia, Sweden and Russia, defeated Napoleon's Grande Armée at Leipzig in Saxony over four days in October 1813, and the French withdrew to France.

The Boeotians led by the Thebans defeated Sparta and its allies at Leuctra in Boeotia on 6 July 371 BCE, after a dispute over renewing the King's Peace, and Spartan influence over Greece was shattered.
Edmund Ollier Publication date 1882, Public domain

British and Allied forces landed at Diego-Suarez on 5 May 1942 and then took the rest of the Vichy French-held island of Madagascar, to keep Japanese ships from its ports; an armistice came on 6 November.

Roman and Pergamene forces under the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus and Eumenes II defeated the Seleucid army of Antiochus III near Magnesia ad Sipylum in Asia Minor, which led to the Treaty of Apamea.
On 26 August 1071 the Seljuk army of Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine army of Romanos IV Diogenes near Manzikert in eastern Anatolia and captured the emperor, and civil strife in Byzantium followed.

French forces under the First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte beat Michael von Melas's Austrian army near Alessandria in Piedmont on 14 June 1800 after a near defeat, and the Austrians left north-western Italy.

Francis I of France, with German landsknechts and late-arriving Venetian allies, defeated the Swiss Confederacy near Melegnano, south-east of Milan, in September 1515; the Perpetual Peace of 1516 followed.

Two United States carrier groups sank all four Japanese fleet carriers present near Midway Atoll in June 1942, six months after Pearl Harbor, and wrecked Admiral Yamamoto's plan to capture the atoll and destroy the American carriers.
USN, photographed from USS Pensacola (CA-24), Public domain

Takeda Shingen's army overran Tokugawa Ieyasu and his Oda allies on the plain of Mikatagahara in Tōtōmi Province on 25 January 1573, while Shingen marched towards Kyoto; Ieyasu escaped to Hamamatsu, and Shingen turned back.

The Ottoman army under Suleiman the Magnificent defeated the Hungarian army of King Louis II near Mohács in 1526; Louis died in flight, and Hungary was later divided between the Ottomans, the Habsburgs and an eastern kingdom.

Greek marines under the Spartan king Leotychides landed at Mount Mycale on the coast of Ionia in 479 BCE, routed the Persian force there and burned its fleet, helping to end Xerxes' invasion of Greece.

A Seljuk army under Sultan Kilij Arslan II ambushed the Byzantine army of Emperor Manuel I Komnenos in a mountain pass west of Iconium in 1176, ending Byzantine efforts to recover the Anatolian interior.

In June 1575 the allied armies of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated Takeda Katsuyori's army near Nagashino Castle in Mikawa Province, Japan, killing many Takeda generals and making Nobunaga's unification of Japan seem certain.
Unknown author (Edo period, circa 18th century), Public domain

A British, French and Russian fleet under Admiral Codrington defeated and largely destroyed an Ottoman and Egyptian fleet at anchor in Navarino Bay in 1827, during the Greek War of Independence, which made Greek independence much more…

An allied crusader army of French, Hungarians and others, with Venetian ships on the Danube, was routed by an Ottoman force under Bayezid I at Nicopolis in 1396, which ended the siege and left the Ottomans stronger in the Balkans.

United States Army and Marine Corps forces invaded Okinawa on 1 April 1945 and, after 82 days against the Japanese Thirty-Second Army, took the island at a cost that fell most heavily on its Okinawan civilians.
Staff Sergent Walter F. Kleine, Public domain

On 6 August 1777 Loyalists and Britain's Indigenous allies ambushed an American militia column and Oneida warriors under Nicholas Herkimer near Oriska, stopping the relief of Fort Stanwix, though the siege was abandoned two weeks later.

In August 479 BCE a Spartan-led Greek alliance defeated the Achaemenid army of Mardonius near Plataea in Boeotia, killing Mardonius and trapping much of his army in its camp, which ended the second Persian invasion of Greece.

An Anglo-Gascon army under Edward, the Black Prince, defeated a larger French army under King John II south of Poitiers in 1356, during the Hundred Years' War, and captured the king, which led to a truce and the Treaty of Brétigny.

A Russian army under Tsar Peter I defeated a Swedish army commanded by Carl Gustaf Rehnskiöld near Poltava in Ukraine on 8 July 1709, the largest battle of the Great Northern War; the rest of the Swedish army surrendered three days later.

French troops under Charles de Lorencez failed three times to storm the Mexican forts of Loreto and Guadalupe above Puebla on 5 May 1862, during the second French intervention in Mexico, and withdrew to Orizaba to await reinforcements.

Roman legions under the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus defeated King Perseus of Macedon and his phalanx near Pydna in 168 BCE, in the Third Macedonian War, ending the Antigonid line of kings and Macedonian independence.

Ptolemy IV of Egypt defeated Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire near Raphia on 22 June 217 BCE, in the Fourth Syrian War, and kept Coele-Syria for Egypt until Antiochus took it back at Panium in 200 BCE.

An Almoravid army under Yusuf ibn Tashfin, joined by the taifa kings of al-Andalus, defeated Alfonso VI of Castile near Badajoz in October 1086, easing Christian pressure on the taifas and opening the way for Almoravid rule in al-Andalus.

An Allied Greek fleet under Themistocles defeated a larger Achaemenid fleet under King Xerxes in the straits between the island of Salamis and the mainland in 480 BCE, after which Xerxes withdrew with much of his army.

A Texian army under Sam Houston defeated Antonio López de Santa Anna's Mexican force in about 18 minutes at San Jacinto in Texas on 21 April 1836, the last battle of the Texas Revolution, and Santa Anna was captured the next day.

Prussian and allied German armies under Moltke surrounded the French Army of Châlons at Sedan in the Franco-Prussian War, forced its surrender with Napoleon III on 2 September 1870, and the Second Empire fell two days later.

China's National Revolutionary Army and Japan's Imperial Army fought for Shanghai from August to November 1937, in the Second Sino-Japanese War; Japan took the city at heavy cost to both sides and advanced on Nanjing.

United States Marines landed on Betio, the main island of Tarawa Atoll in the Gilbert Islands, on 20 November 1943 and took it from its Japanese garrison in 76 hours at a cost of nearly 6,400 lives on all sides.
USMC Archives from Quantico, USA, CC BY 2.0

Julius Caesar's army defeated the Optimate forces of Quintus Caecilius Metellus Scipio and King Juba I of Numidia near Thapsus in North Africa on 6 April 46 BCE, in the last civil war of the Roman Republic.

A German offensive through the Ardennes in Belgium and Luxembourg took the Western Allies by surprise on 16 December 1944 but was halted short of the Meuse, and the front was restored by the end of January 1945.

A coalition led by the Roman general Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I fought the Huns and their vassals under Attila in Gaul in 451 CE; Theodoric was killed, Attila withdrew, and the outcome is disputed.

In May 334 BCE Alexander the Great of Macedon defeated the field army of the Persian satraps of Asia Minor at the crossing of the Granicus in the Troad, the first of his three major battles with the Achaemenid Empire.
Charles Le Brun / Abraham Genoels, Public domain

Alexander the Great's Macedonian army crossed the swollen Hydaspes in May 326 BCE and defeated the Pauravas under Porus on its bank in what is now Punjab, Pakistan; Alexander spared Porus and made him a satrap.
